passage: I'm Lokesh, and I live across the lane from Dolma. Every evening for months I saw Dolma on the front steps, scrolling, head bent, not even looking up when the ball rolled past. Then something changed. Last month I saw Dolma at the end of the lane with a borrowed bat, asking if there was room in our neighbourhood cricket game. At half past five each day since, there's been a figure in the field, chasing badly at first. And on Saturday mornings I've seen Dolma leave with a guitar case. I don't know if Dolma misses the phone. But the front steps are empty in the evenings now, and I've heard Dolma laughing.

qa.q: What two activities did Dolma sign up for?
qa.a: Evening cricket and a Saturday guitar class.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling about the empty hours before joining?
qa.a: Bored and restless, though Lokesh can only guess; the scrolling on the steps and the later laughter hint at a change.

qa.q: What else could help Dolma stay with the new habits, and why?
qa.a: Invite a friend to join the guitar class, since company makes new routines easier to keep.

qa.q: How does the change look to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh, who plays in the lane, gains a new player and sees the steps empty, and is glad to hear laughter even without knowing what Dolma felt.

grounding: A teen signs up for evening cricket and a weekend guitar class so the free hours are filled.

passage:
Week one, Monday: Nitin's phone is in the drawer, as he promised himself. By seven he is lying on the bed staring at the fan. There is nothing to do. By eight the phone is back in his hand.
Week two, Thursday: Himani, from the flat below, bangs on the door with a tennis ball. “We're one short for cricket in the compound. Six to seven-thirty, every day. Coming?” He goes. He's terrible. He comes back sweaty and hungry, eats, does his homework, and is asleep by ten-thirty without noticing the phone.
Week four, Saturday: His first guitar class at the music school near the market, ten to eleven. His fingers hurt. He practises the two chords for an hour that afternoon instead of scrolling, mostly because he wants to show Himani on Monday.

qa.q: What time does the compound cricket run?
What was Nitin feeling on Monday of week one, staring at the fan?
qa.a: Nitin felt bored and restless, with nothing to fill the gap, so the phone quickly came back.

qa.q: Why did cricket and guitar work where the drawer alone did not?
qa.a: They filled the empty hours with something fun and social, so there was no boring gap for the phone to fill.

qa.q: What might the change mean for Himani?
qa.a: Himani gains a player for the short side and someone keen to show off new chords, a small friendship growing from it.

grounding: Shows a teen filling evenings with cricket with neighbours and weekends with a guitar class, since simply removing the phone left a boring gap.

passage:
Rehana, your father was just like you at fifteen, only his screen was the video-game box plugged into our television. Every evening, four, five hours. We tried hiding the cable. He sulked on the sofa, bored stiff, and found the cable within two days. Taking the game away didn't work, because nothing took its place.
Then your grandfather did something clever. The colony boys played cricket on the maidan every evening, and he walked your father there and said, “You bowl, beta, you have the height.” And on Sundays I sent him to Master Joseph's guitar class, because he was always drumming on the dining table anyway.
Within a month he was coming home at seven, sweaty and starving, and falling asleep over dinner. The game box gathered dust. Nobody had to hide anything.
So when you tell me there's nothing to do but your phone, I, your Minakshi Dadi, say: let's find your cricket.

qa.q: Where did Rehana's father go on Sundays?
How did Rehana's father feel when the cable was hidden?
qa.a: He was bored and sulky, stuck on the sofa with nothing to do, so he hunted the cable down.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the habit?
qa.a: The grandfather taking him to the colony cricket and sending him to the Sunday guitar class, which filled the evenings instead of just removing the game.

qa.q: How might the grandfather have seen his plan working?
qa.a: He probably felt quietly pleased, seeing his son come home sweaty and happy with no need to hide anything.

grounding: An elder recalls her son's screen habit fading once evening cricket and a weekend guitar class filled the hours that removing the game had left empty.
